record.ear: Fair and cold. High 30. Low 21. The year came in clear at midnight.

lead.headline: Queens takes the New Year at midnight before the Society's 40 recorders
lead.deck: Some 31,000 at Queens Plaza, Jamaica Avenue and Main Street; Times Square carried in the Record's window from 11:30 p.m.; nine arrests, none for gunfire
lead.body: The New Year was received at midnight in Queens by crowds the police estimated at 31,000 at the three centres, and by the 40 recording parties of the Phonautograph Society of Queens, stationed from Long Island City to Far Rockaway. The Times Square crowd was carried by wire to the Record's Jackson Avenue window from 11:30 p.m. Inspector Arthur Kane reports nine arrests, eight for drunkenness and one concerning a coal horse. No gunfire was recorded. The elevated ran every eight minutes until 4 a.m.

columns.headline: Governor-elect Roosevelt to take the oath at Albany at noon today
columns.body: Mr. Franklin D. Roosevelt will take the oath as Governor at noon today in the Assembly Chamber at Albany, succeeding Governor Smith. The ceremony will be carried by wire to the Record's window and to the Queens County Court House. The Legislature convenes tomorrow.

columns.headline: Byrd's party reports the first hut raised at Little America
columns.body: Commander Byrd's message, received at Bay Shore at 2:40 a.m. yesterday, reports the frame of the first hut raised at Little America and the dogs hauling stores from the ships in relays of eight miles. The Commander asks that greetings be sent to the families of the men.

columns.headline: Newark valve works reopens tomorrow; Arcade expects 400 sleeves Thursday
columns.body: The Newark works that supplies most of the borough's receiving valves reopens tomorrow after its Christmas closing. The Vantry Arcade's hardware counter expects 400 six-sleeves on Thursday and will then lift its limit. Used valves were 40 cents on Jackson Avenue yesterday. Eggs are 64 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Phonautograph Society's 40 midnight records were delivered to its Jamaica office by 3:10 a.m. Mr. Abbot will not play them until all are compared.

speaker.ear: New Year's Day, clear and cold. High 30. Every head in Queens is louder than the Hum.

lead.headline: Queens rings in 1929 on forty records and one horse
lead.deck: Thirty-one thousand in the streets, nine arrests, no shooting; the Society's men catch midnight from the Plaza to the Rockaways
lead.body: At the stroke of twelve the Society's forty men lifted their machines, and Queens did what it always does, only on the record. Thirty-one thousand people kissed, sang and blew horns at the three centres. Nine were arrested, eight for drink and one for riding a coal horse up the Jamaica Avenue steps, which the horse had not agreed to. Nobody fired a gun, because the Health Department said it would be heard. The forty records are at the Society's office. The headaches are at home.

columns.headline: Roosevelt takes the oath, and Albany swears it heard him
columns.body: Franklin Roosevelt became Governor at noon today in the Assembly Chamber with his hand on the old Dutch family Bible, and the Record's window carried every word down the wire to Jackson Avenue. Governor Smith went home. The Legislature opens tomorrow, and the Listening Act is waiting by the door.

columns.headline: Little America raises the roof, and the dogs do the heavy lifting
columns.body: Byrd's men have the frame of their first hut up on the Barrier, eight miles from the ships, and the dogs are hauling everything else. The Commander sends New Year's greetings to the families at home. The dogs send theirs to the seals, who are less grateful.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'What were my New Year's resolutions?'
columns.body: Sir, at 12:40 this morning you rang position 12 to tell her you would never drink again, and at 12:55 you rang her to ask the way home. She wrote neither down. Your building, however, is not so discreet. We would not ask it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Society has all forty records and will not play one until it has heard the other boroughs'. Fair is fair.

record.ear: Cloudy and milder. High 36. Low 27. Ice at Whitestone eleven inches.

lead.headline: Five boroughs' midnight records compared; Queens loudest for 11 seconds
lead.deck: Mayor's office plays the records of the city's 212 public buildings; Brooklyn longest, Richmond shortest, the Bronx 'early by a clock'
lead.body: The Mayor's office yesterday compared the midnight records of the city's 212 public buildings, as was done for the Armistice silence. Manhattan's noise held at its height for nine minutes and Brooklyn's for fourteen. Queens was the loudest borough for eleven seconds after 12:00, a margin the clerks attributed to a train on the elevated at Queensboro Plaza. The Bronx began at 11:58 by the Courthouse clock. Richmond's peak lasted three minutes and ended with a ferry whistle. The records go to the Municipal Archives.

columns.headline: Governor Roosevelt takes the oath; Legislature convenes at noon today
columns.body: Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt was sworn at noon yesterday in the Assembly Chamber before some 2,000 persons. The Legislature convenes at noon today and will receive the Governor's annual message. Senator Edmund Harlan says the Listening Act will be reported from his committee 'after the 9th.'

columns.headline: Newark valve works reopens this morning after the Christmas closing
columns.body: The Newark works reopens at 7 this morning with 640 hands, the company wired the Arcade's hardware counter last night, and the first motor truck for Queens will leave at 3 p.m. The counter expects 400 six-sleeves tomorrow. Eggs are 63 cents, coal 15 dollars.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society receives all 40 midnight records; one party late
columns.body: All 40 recording parties of the Phonautograph Society of Queens had delivered their records to the Jamaica office by 3:10 a.m. yesterday, the Far Rockaway party last, having walked from the beach. Mr. Cyril Abbot says the records will go into the 1978 case 'after review.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board of Elections will receive the Riverhead returns by wire at 10 a.m. tomorrow and by paper at 2 p.m.

speaker.ear: Cloudy and milder. High 36. The year is two days old and already behind on its bills.

lead.headline: Queens out-shouts the city by eleven seconds, and the elevated takes a bow
lead.deck: Brooklyn hollers longest, the Bronx jumps the gun, and Staten Island is drowned out by its own ferry
lead.body: The Mayor's men played every borough's midnight back yesterday and Queens won, briefly. For eleven seconds after twelve we were the loudest place in the city, chiefly because a train went over the Plaza at the stroke and did not care what year it was. Brooklyn hollered for fourteen minutes, which is Brooklyn. The Bronx started two minutes early by its own clock. Staten Island's midnight lasted three minutes, and then a ferry whistle had the last word. Manhattan says it was not trying.

columns.headline: Albany opens for business, and the Listening Act waits on the line
columns.body: The Legislature sat down today and Governor Roosevelt sent up his first message, on farms, water power and the State's roads, and not one word on the Listening Act. Senator Harlan says his committee reports after the 9th. The committee room is listening already.

columns.headline: Newark lights up the valve works, and Queens holds its breath
columns.body: Six hundred and forty hands went back into the Newark valve works at seven this morning, and the first truck leaves for Queens at three. Four hundred sleeves land at the Arcade tomorrow. The pawnbroker on Jackson Avenue is said to have gone very quiet.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Down by Hell Gate, says a tug that heard it go under
columns.body: The mate of the tug Kate Fallon says WORS 1610 came up on the wheelhouse set at two on New Year's morning off Hell Gate, faint, 'as if from under the keel.' He would not swear to it in court. He swore at it, he says, a good deal.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Riverhead goes back on the wire at ten tomorrow and on paper at two. Same ballots, second opinion.

record.ear: Cloudy and mild. High 38. Low 30. Soft ice reported off Willets Point.

lead.headline: Legislature convenes; Governor's message silent on the Listening Act
lead.deck: Message read to both Houses from 1:15 p.m.; Senator Harlan's committee to hear the bill on the 9th; Mr. Pell's request for an unrecorded hearing 'under consideration'
lead.body: The Legislature convened at noon yesterday, and the Governor's annual message was read to both Houses beginning at 1:15 p.m. It treats of water power, the farms, the State's highways and the prisons, and does not mention the Listening Act. Senator Edmund Harlan told the Record that the Judiciary Committee will hear the bill at 10 a.m. on the 9th. Mr. Lucius Pell's request that the committee room's system be disconnected for the day is 'under consideration by the custodian, who is looking for it.'

columns.headline: Board of Elections receives Riverhead returns afresh at 10 and 2 today
columns.body: The Suffolk clerk will send the Riverhead returns to the Board of Elections by wire at 10 this morning and by paper at 2 this afternoon, in the presence of counsel. Mr. Francis Gorman will attend for Mr. Walter Pruitt. The bench warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti remains outstanding.

columns.headline: First Newark valves leave for Queens; Arcade limit to be lifted
columns.body: The first motor truck from the reopened Newark works left at 3:20 p.m. yesterday with 1,100 six-sleeves of receiving valves for Queens counters, 400 of them for the Vantry Arcade. The Arcade's hardware counter will lift its limit at 8 this morning.

columns.headline: Tug's mate reports WORS 1610 off Hell Gate at 2:04 a.m. on the 1st
columns.body: Mr. Peter Sloane, mate of the tug Kate Fallon, told the Radio Division yesterday that a station calling itself WORS 1610 was received off Hell Gate at 2:04 a.m. on the 1st. Mr. Harold Pike went out on the 4 p.m. tide. He received nothing.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reports a temperature of 24 above at noon, local time, and the dogs 'too warm to work.'

speaker.ear: Mild and grey. High 38. The ice men are watching the sky with both eyes.

lead.headline: Riverhead tells it twice, and for once the wire and the paper agree
lead.deck: Same count by wire at ten and by paper at two; counsel listen to both and find nothing to argue about, which upsets them
lead.body: The Suffolk clerk sent Riverhead down the wire at ten this morning and down the road on paper at two, and the Board sat and listened to both. They matched, vote for vote. Counsel looked at each other. Chairman Delaney said Mr. Hoover's majority was not affected, from habit. The only difference was the clock: the wire ran eleven seconds longer than the clerk did, and nobody asked what was in them. Walter Pruitt's name was in neither. Joseph Marchetti's was in neither either. The warrant is still out.

columns.headline: Valves are back, the limit is off, and the Arcade queue is a party line
columns.body: Four hundred sleeves hit the Arcade counter at eight this morning and the limit came off at five past. By noon two hundred had gone. Men stood in line describing their sets to each other like grandchildren. The price is a dollar and four. The pawnbroker is selling neckties.

columns.headline: Hell Gate tug picks up WORS; the Radio man takes the tide and gets static
columns.body: The Kate Fallon's mate says WORS 1610 came up off Hell Gate on New Year's morning. Mr. Pike of the Radio Division rowed out on the four o'clock tide and heard the river, a ferry and his own teeth. He has asked for a warmer boat.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a New Year's proposal in Sunnyside, heard twice
columns.body: Darlings, a certain young man of 43rd Street proposed at midnight to a certain young lady, and was accepted, and then proposed again at 12:20 to make sure. Her mother's parlour caught both. We are told the second was better. The first had the elevated in it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pell says a room that cannot be switched off should be carried out. Albany says it is a committee room, not a trunk.

record.ear: Mild and cloudy. High 41. Low 33. Whitestone ice ten inches; cutting slowed.

lead.headline: Riverhead returns received afresh; wire and paper agree to the vote
lead.deck: Wire transmission timed at 4 minutes 11 seconds against the clerk's 4 minutes; Board certifies Suffolk; Mr. Pruitt's name 'in neither'
lead.body: The Riverhead returns of November 6 were received by the Board of Elections by wire at 10:02 a.m. yesterday and by paper at 2:05 p.m., and agree to the vote. The Board's clerk timed the wire transmission at 4 minutes 11 seconds; the Suffolk clerk timed his sending at 4 minutes. Chairman Delaney said the difference 'is not a vote' and certified the Suffolk returns. Mr. Francis Gorman noted that Mr. Walter Pruitt's name appears in neither. Justice Rourke rules on Mr. Pruitt's petition on Monday.

columns.headline: Exchange cat receives a second parcel, again postmarked Corona
columns.body: A second parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was delivered yesterday, containing a tin of sardines and postmarked Corona, January 2. The supervisor reports the address 'in the same hand' as the first. The cat was present at the opening.

columns.headline: Arcade sells 260 sleeves of valves in a day after lifting its limit
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade's hardware counter sold 260 six-sleeves of receiving valves yesterday after lifting its limit at 8:05 a.m., the counterman reports, at 1 dollar 04. Used valves fell to 15 cents on Jackson Avenue. Eggs are 62 cents the dozen.

columns.headline: Senate takes up the Kellogg treaty; vote expected within the fortnight
columns.body: The Senate began on the general treaty for the renunciation of war yesterday, Senator Borah opening for the Foreign Relations Committee. A vote is expected within the fortnight. The State Department has asked that the vote be recorded on the Senate's own system 'for the treaty archive.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Commander Byrd reports 41 tons of stores hauled to Little America by dog team since Monday.

speaker.ear: Mild. High 41. The Sound is going soft, and so is the price of valves.

lead.headline: Party Line's secret admirer rings twice: more sardines from Corona
lead.deck: Same careful hand, same tin, same no-name; the operators open it on position 43 and the cat keeps her own counsel
lead.body: Somebody in Corona means it. A second parcel came for Party Line at the exchange yesterday, in the same careful hand, with the same tin of sardines inside and no name. The supervisor opened it in front of the cat, and the cat ate four. Forty operators have a theory each. We have one too, and we are not printing it, because the Speaker does not guess about Corona in a month like this. Whoever you are: she says thank you. She does not, but we do.

columns.headline: Riverhead's wire runs eleven seconds over, and the Board calls time
columns.body: The wire count and the paper count agreed vote for vote, but the wire ran four minutes and eleven seconds against the clerk's four minutes flat. Chairman Delaney says eleven seconds is 'not a vote.' It is long enough to say a good deal, Mr. Chairman.

columns.headline: Valves fall off the shelf, and the pawnbroker falls off his perch
columns.body: Two hundred and sixty sleeves went over the Arcade counter yesterday, and the second-hand valve on Jackson Avenue dropped from forty cents to fifteen in one afternoon. Eggs are sixty-two cents the dozen, and nobody is buying them second-hand.

columns.headline: Senate gets on the line to outlaw war, and Borah does the talking
columns.body: The Senate has started on the Kellogg treaty, which outlaws war in every language but the one people fight in. Senator Borah opened. The vote is expected within a fortnight, and the State Department wants it on the record so the future can hear who said aye.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Forty-one tons hauled at Little America by dog. The dogs want it known it was not forty.

record.ear: Cloudy, milder. High 40. Low 31. Whitestone field ten inches; cutting slowed.

lead.headline: Phonautograph Society divides 19 to 17 on the carol record for 1978
lead.deck: Members' meeting at the Jamaica office sits until 11:20 p.m.; Mrs. Ottoline Grieve objects to 'a record of nowhere' in a case for Queens; Mr. Abbot casts no vote
lead.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens voted 19 to 17 last night to admit to its 1978 case the second Woodside record of the carol heard on WORS 1610 on Christmas night. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve, who moved its exclusion, said the case was 'for Queens, and a record of nowhere cannot be of Queens.' Mr. Edgar Linde answered that it was received in Woodside 'and that is somewhere.' Mr. Cyril Abbot did not vote. Mrs. Grieve has asked that her objection be recorded and placed beside it.

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,840 sleeves of valves sold at Queens counters
columns.body: Queens hardware counters sold 1,840 six-sleeves of receiving valves in the three days since Newark reopened, by the Record's canvass of 22 dealers, against none in the week before. The Arcade sold its 400 and has reordered. Used valves are 12 cents. Eggs are 62 cents.

columns.headline: Answering dolls examined at Newark; maker reports 'nothing to correct'
columns.body: The Newark maker of the answering doll wired the Vantry Arcade's toy shop yesterday that the three dolls returned on December 20 have been examined and 'found to say six words at the works.' The maker states there is 'nothing to correct.'

columns.headline: Mr. Lasko's case to the grand jury on Tuesday; fur coat not found
columns.body: The case of Mr. Victor Lasko, held in the Christmas Eve burglary of the Hale house in Jackson Heights, goes to the Queens grand jury on Tuesday. Detective Sergeant Edward Moran says the fur coat, worth 400 dollars, has not been found at any pawnshop in the borough.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Justice Rourke rules on Mr. Walter Pruitt's petition at 10 a.m. Monday in Long Island City.

speaker.ear: Milder. High 40. The ice is thinning, and so is everyone's patience.

lead.headline: Society splits 19 to 17 over a carol from out of town
lead.deck: Mrs. Grieve says the 1978 box is for Queens only and WORS is from nowhere; the box gets the carol and her complaint
lead.body: Thirty-six members of the Phonautograph Society spent last night arguing whether a Christmas carol nobody can name, from a station nobody can find, belongs in a box for 1978. Nineteen said yes. Seventeen said no, led by Mrs. Ottoline Grieve of Kew Gardens, who says the box is for Queens and the carol is from nowhere. Mr. Linde said Woodside heard it, so it is from Woodside. Mr. Abbot sat on his hands. Mrs. Grieve's objection goes in the box too, so 1978 can hear us quarrel.

columns.headline: Newark says the chatty dolls were perfectly quiet at home
columns.body: The three answering dolls who came to Queens saying seven words have been examined in Newark, where they say six. The maker finds 'nothing to correct.' So the dolls behave at the works and speak up in the Arcade. Every mother in Queens knows that doll.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Has anybody rung about a fur coat?'
columns.body: Madam, no. But if a lady in Corona or thereabouts rings the exchange to ask what a good fur coat fetches, the operator will connect her, as is her duty, and the operator will remember, as is her nature. Sergeant Moran sends his regards.

columns.headline: Valves sell like hot cakes, which are also up
columns.body: Eighteen hundred and forty sleeves of valves went over Queens counters in three days, the Record counted, and we believe it, being busy. The Arcade has reordered. Used ones are twelve cents, and the pawnbroker is said to be listening to his own stock.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Justice Rourke rules on Pruitt Monday at ten. The ledger has been told to dress warmly.

editorial.headline: She rings in the New Year at the Hartley Building
editorial.body: While decent people sang Auld Lang Syne, the Hartley Insurance Building on Queens Plaza rang with the sound of eighty stenographers leaving it. They had been locked in since Christmas Eve on the orders of Mr. Silas Hartley to finish the annual returns, sleeping on the filing cabinets, paid for a day of eight hours. At midnight the doors of every floor were found unlocked and garlanded with black ribbon, and the night watchman was found in the lift, asleep and smiling, a silk scarf for a pillow. Mr. Hartley says the returns are late. This paper says a stenographer's place is at her machine. Our own stenographer, Miss Penrose, says she would like a word.

record.ear: Rain early, then clearing. High 44. Water standing on the Willets Point field.

lead.headline: Miss Honora Quigley, Queens operator from 1883, buried at Calvary
lead.deck: Placed the first call through the Long Island City exchange; 61 operators at the graveside; the exchange observes a minute's silence at all positions at 10 a.m.
lead.body: Miss Honora Quigley, who placed the first call through the Long Island City exchange in 1883 and retired as chief operator in 1921, was buried at Calvary Cemetery yesterday after a Requiem Mass at St. Mary's, Vernon Boulevard. She was 72, and died on New Year's Day of pneumonia. Sixty-one operators attended. At 10 a.m. the Queens exchange held a minute's silence at all positions, during which, the supervisor reports, eleven calls waited without complaint. Party Line was carried to position 1.

columns.headline: Little America to be heard nightly at 10 in the Record's window
columns.body: The Record will play the night's message from Little America in its Jackson Avenue window at 10 p.m. daily, the Navy at Bay Shore having arranged a regular schedule with Commander Byrd's operator. Last night's message reported the second hut roofed and 88 dogs 'in good order.'

columns.headline: Kissena Lake skating races postponed; ice four inches and wet
columns.body: The Queens Skating Club's quarter-mile and mile races, set for today on Kissena Lake, are postponed, the Park Department finding the ice at four inches with water on the north shore. Mr. Wilbur Ames, secretary, says the races will be held 'at the first hard frost.'

columns.headline: Ice harvest stands at 31,200 tons; Willets Point field closed by rain
columns.body: The three Sound ice companies have housed 31,200 tons since November, the Bowery Bay company reports, cutting having resumed on December 29. The Willets Point field closed at noon yesterday for standing water. Whitestone cut until 3 p.m. at ten inches.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Kellogg treaty debate resumes in the Senate tomorrow. Senator Borah expects a vote 'within the fortnight.'

speaker.ear: Rain, then clearing. High 44. The Sound is wearing a puddle for a hat.

lead.headline: Honora Quigley, the first voice on the line, is put through for the last time
lead.deck: She connected Queens in 1883 and never once told what she heard; sixty-one operators and one cat see her off
lead.body: Miss Honora Quigley said 'Number, please' to Long Island City in 1883, before most of the borough had a number to give her, and she said it for thirty-eight years. She was chief operator when she retired, and she was seventy-two when pneumonia carried her off on New Year's Day. Sixty-one operators stood at Calvary yesterday. At ten the whole exchange went silent for a minute, and eleven callers waited without a word, which she would have liked. She heard everything. She repeated nothing. We could learn.

columns.headline: Little America goes on the air nightly, and Jackson Avenue gets the best seat
columns.body: Byrd's camp will be played in the Record's Jackson Avenue window at ten every night, the Navy having fixed a schedule. Last night: a second hut roofed and eighty-eight dogs in good order. Bring a thermos. The dogs bring their own fur.

columns.headline: Kissena ice too thin to race on, so the skaters skate around the subject
columns.body: The Queens Skating Club's races on Kissena Lake are off, the ice being four inches and wet on the north shore. Mr. Ames, the secretary, says they will race at the first hard frost. Until then the club meets indoors and argues about who would have won.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike goes back on the river and picks up a cold
columns.body: Mr. Pike of the Radio Division went back on the East River last night and spent three hours off Hell Gate. He received a head cold and the Astoria ferry. WORS 1610, if it was there, kept its counsel. The tug's mate says it is shy of strangers.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Pruitt's ruling tomorrow at ten. Marchetti is invited. Marchetti has not replied.

record.ear: Unseasonably mild. High 54. Low 40. Fog on the Sound tonight.

lead.headline: January thaw stops ice cutting on the Sound; 52 degrees at noon Sunday
lead.deck: Highest January reading at the Weather Bureau since 1913; Whitestone field down to eight inches; 210 men laid off a second time
lead.body: The thermometer at the Weather Bureau stood at 52 degrees at noon yesterday, the highest January reading since 1913, and the three Sound ice companies stopped cutting at 1 p.m. The Whitestone field measured eight inches, with standing water to the shore. The Bowery Bay Ice Company laid off its 210 men a second time, with a day's pay. Mr. Owen Pratt said the harvest at 31,200 tons is 'eleven thousand short of a summer.' The Bureau gives mild weather through Thursday.

columns.headline: Justice Rourke to rule on Mr. Pruitt's petition at 10 this morning
columns.body: Justice Thaddeus Rourke will give his decision on Mr. Walter Pruitt's petition at 10 this morning in Long Island City. Mr. Joseph Marchetti, for whom a bench warrant is outstanding, has not been found. Mr. Francis Gorman will ask that the Riverhead ledger be corrected.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five beat the Bay Ridge Celtics 31 to 28
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club five beat the Bay Ridge Celtics 31 to 28 at the armory on Saturday night before 1,250, Mr. Frank Dillon scoring 12. A disputed basket was settled by the armory's record, played to both benches. The club stands six and four.

columns.headline: Kid Sorrentino outpoints Harry Lusk in ten rounds at Ridgewood Grove
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino of Astoria won a decision over Harry Lusk of Jersey City in ten rounds at Ridgewood Grove on Saturday night before 3,400. The judges' cards were read to the house and recorded. Mr. Lusk's manager has asked for the record of the seventh round.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reported 'snow, wind, all well' at 9:58 p.m. The crowd at the Record's window was 600.

speaker.ear: Fifty-four in January. Fog tonight. The ice men are fishing for their jobs.

lead.headline: Judge strikes Pruitt off the ledger and leaves Marchetti on the line
lead.deck: Justice Rourke orders 10:31 ruled through in red and a note written in; the lineman is still wanted and still missing
lead.body: Justice Rourke ruled at ten this morning that Walter Pruitt did not write the Riverhead entry of 10:31 on election night, and ordered the ledger corrected in red ink with a note giving the reason. Mr. Pruitt thanked his lawyer and went out into the fog. The judge said he could not rule on why Joseph Marchetti wrote it, Mr. Marchetti not having been 'kind enough to tell us.' The bench warrant stands. Somewhere a lineman is reading this and keeping his receiver on the hook.

columns.headline: Thaw puts the Sound on hold, and the ice men go home wet
columns.body: Fifty-two degrees on Sunday, the warmest January noon since 1913, and the Sound has turned to slush with a crust on it. Bowery Bay has sent its 210 men home again. Mr. Pratt says the harvest is eleven thousand tons short of a summer. Buy your ice now.

columns.headline: Club five beat Bay Ridge, and the armory replays the argument
columns.body: The Athletic Club five beat the Bay Ridge Celtics 31 to 28 on Saturday, a disputed basket being played back from the armory's record to both benches, who each heard what they wanted. Dillon scored twelve. Six won, four lost, and nobody hoarse for once.

columns.headline: Kid Sorrentino wins on points, and Lusk's man wants round seven played back
columns.body: Kid Sorrentino of Astoria won ten rounds from Harry Lusk at Ridgewood Grove on Saturday. Lusk's manager wants the record of the seventh, in which he says something was said that was not boxing. Three thousand four hundred heard it. None of them is saying.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Riverhead ledger now has a red line through 10:31. Marchetti has a red line through everything.

record.ear: Fog, then mild. High 50. Low 41. The Weather Bureau gives no frost before Friday.

lead.headline: Justice Rourke orders the Riverhead 10:31 entry corrected; Mr. Pruitt cleared
lead.deck: Decision read at 10:06 a.m.; ledger to carry a red line and a note of the order; bench warrant for Mr. Marchetti 'stands until he does'
lead.body: Justice Thaddeus Rourke ruled at 10:06 a.m. yesterday that the Riverhead ledger entry of 10:31 p.m. on November 6 was not made by Mr. Walter Pruitt, and ordered the Suffolk clerk to rule it through in red ink and note the order beneath. The Justice said the court 'cannot find a purpose for the entry, the writer not being present to supply one.' The bench warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti 'stands until he does,' the Justice said.

columns.headline: Listening Act hearing tomorrow at 10; committee room's system still connected
columns.body: The Senate Judiciary Committee hears the Listening Act at 10 tomorrow in Room 332 of the Capitol. The custodian, Mr. Amos Teller, reports that he has traced the room's 1911 system to a wall behind the press gallery 'and no further.' Mr. Lucius Pell will attend.

columns.headline: Lasko case before the grand jury today; parlour record to be played
columns.body: The Queens grand jury will hear the case of Mr. Victor Lasko today, the District Attorney's office says, including the parlour record of the Hale house of Christmas Eve, two hours ten minutes. Mr. Leonard Hale will testify. The fur coat has not been found.

columns.headline: Valves 98 cents the sleeve as Newark ships 3,000; eggs 60
columns.body: The Newark works shipped 3,000 six-sleeves of receiving valves to Queens counters last week, the company reports, and the price at the Vantry Arcade fell yesterday to 98 cents, the first below a dollar since November. Eggs are 60 cents, butter 58.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Senate leaders expect a vote on the Kellogg treaty on the 15th.

speaker.ear: Fog and fifty. High 50. January has forgotten its lines.

lead.headline: Grand jury hears the parlour, and the parlour does the talking
lead.deck: Two hours of a dark house on Christmas Eve, one voice and one spaniel; Lasko is indicted and the fur coat is still out
lead.body: The grand jury sat in a dark room this afternoon and listened to two hours and ten minutes of the Hale parlour on Christmas Eve, most of it a clock and a spaniel, and twelve seconds of it a man saying 'It's only Vic, Brownie.' They needed forty minutes to indict Victor Lasko for burglary. His lawyer says a room cannot testify. The District Attorney says it just did. The silver is back on 81st Street. The fur coat is still out somewhere, keeping someone warm.

columns.headline: Albany's custodian follows the wire to a wall, and the wall hangs up
columns.body: Mr. Amos Teller, custodian at the Capitol, has traced the 1911 system in Room 332 to a wall behind the press gallery, and there it stops. Mr. Pell wanted it off for tomorrow's hearing on listening. The room will be listening to the hearing on listening.

columns.headline: Valves drop under a dollar, and the borough tunes back in
columns.body: A sleeve of valves is ninety-eight cents at the Arcade, the first price under a dollar since November, Newark having sent over three thousand sleeves. Eggs are sixty. Butter is fifty-eight. The pawnbroker is down to twelve cents and taking eggs.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is the Kellogg treaty a party line?'
columns.body: Sir, it is a line with sixty-odd parties on it, every one promising never to pick up a gun again. The Senate votes on the 15th. The operator has heard a great many promises, and she will believe this one when it is played back.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Pruitt went back to work today. Somebody brought a cake. The cake has been entered in no ledger.

record.ear: Mild and cloudy. High 47. Low 38. Kissena Lake closed to skaters.

lead.headline: Mr. Lasko indicted for the Hale burglary after the parlour record is played
lead.deck: Grand jury hears 2 hours 10 minutes of the 81st Street record and deliberates 40 minutes; arraignment Friday; fur coat 'still sought'
lead.body: The Queens grand jury returned an indictment for burglary in the first degree against Mr. Victor Lasko, 29, of Corona, at 4:15 p.m. yesterday, after hearing the parlour record of the Hale house of Christmas Eve in full and the testimony of Mr. Leonard Hale. It deliberated 40 minutes. Mr. Lasko's counsel, Mr. Saul Feder, said he will move to exclude the record 'under the law as it stands and the law as it is proposed.' Arraignment is set for Friday. The fur coat is still sought.

columns.headline: Senate Judiciary Committee hears the Listening Act at 10 today in Room 332
columns.body: The Judiciary Committee will hear the Listening Act at 10 this morning. Witnesses listed are Mr. Lucius Pell for the Queens Real Estate Owners' Association, Mr. Cyril Abbot for the Phonautograph Society and Detective Sergeant Edward Moran of Queens. A stenographer will attend. The room's system remains connected.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society places 39 midnight records in the 1978 case
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens placed 39 of its 40 midnight records in the third copper case yesterday, with the WORS 1610 carol record and Mrs. Ottoline Grieve's recorded objection to it. Record No. 23, from the Maspeth party, was not placed. Mr. Cyril Abbot declined to say why.

columns.headline: Little America: forty seconds of Barrier wind played in the window
columns.body: Last night's message from Little America, played at 10 in the Record's window to about 400, included forty seconds of the wind on the Barrier recorded at the camp at Commander Byrd's direction, 'so that Queens may know.' The temperature on Jackson Avenue was 46.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve has asked that record No. 23 be played at the Society's next members' meeting.

speaker.ear: Mild and grey. High 47. Albany is colder, and it is not the weather.

lead.headline: Albany hears the Listening Act, and Room 332 hears Albany
lead.deck: Pell asks for the switch, the custodian shrugs, the stenographer writes it down, and a 1911 wall takes down every word for free
lead.body: The Judiciary Committee sat this morning on whether a room may testify, in a room that was testifying the whole time. Mr. Pell began by asking again for the system to be switched off. The custodian pointed at a wall. Mr. Pell spoke for an hour and twenty minutes with his back to it. Mr. Abbot spoke for twenty, facing it. Sergeant Moran played the Hale parlour, and a Queens spaniel was heard in the Capitol. The committee reports on the 16th. The wall has the minutes.

columns.headline: Lasko indicted, and his lawyer wants the record struck off the record
columns.body: Victor Lasko was indicted yesterday after forty minutes, and Mr. Feder, his lawyer, will move to keep the Hale parlour out of court under the law as it is and the law as it may be. That covers a lot of law. Arraignment Friday. The fur coat sends no word.

columns.headline: Society boxes up midnight for 1978, minus one Maspeth record
columns.body: Thirty-nine midnights went into the Society's copper case yesterday, with the WORS carol and Mrs. Grieve's objection. The fortieth, from Maspeth, did not. Mr. Abbot will not say why. Mrs. Grieve wants it played at the next meeting. The box is getting more interesting than the borough.

columns.headline: Byrd sends home forty seconds of wind, and Jackson Avenue gets the chills
columns.body: Last night the Record's window played forty seconds of the wind on the Barrier, sent at the Commander's request 'so that Queens may know.' Four hundred people stood on Jackson Avenue in a forty-six-degree thaw and shivered anyway. That is what a good record does.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The committee's stenographer and the room disagree on one word of Mr. Pell's. The room is not taking questions.

record.ear: Mild. High 45. Low 36. Colder from Friday night, the Bureau says.

lead.headline: Listening Act heard in Room 332 with the room's system connected
lead.deck: Mr. Pell's renewed motion denied at 10:04 a.m., no switch being found; committee to report on the 16th; stenographer's minutes and room's record differ at one word
lead.body: Senator Edmund Harlan opened the Judiciary Committee's hearing on the Listening Act yesterday. At 10:04 he denied Mr. Lucius Pell's renewed motion that the room's 1911 system be disconnected, the custodian 'having found a wall but no switch.' Mr. Pell spoke for 81 minutes, Mr. Abbot for 20, and Sergeant Moran played the Hale record. The committee will report on the 16th. The stenographer's minutes and the room's record differ at one word of Mr. Pell's, which the Senator ordered 'left as each has it.'

columns.headline: Mr. Pell before the committee, from the room's record, 11:31 a.m.
columns.body: MR. PELL: 'A building that has listened since 1911 has listened without a licence because there was none. The Act asks it to apply. I ask the committee who signs the application.' SENATOR HARLAN: 'The owner.' MR. PELL: 'Then the committee has not met my clients' buildings.'

columns.headline: Thaw holds a fifth day; Weather Bureau gives frost by Saturday
columns.body: The mild weather held a fifth day yesterday with a high of 47. The Weather Bureau gives a change to colder on Friday night and frost by Saturday. The Bowery Bay Ice Company will recall its men 'the morning the field will bear a horse.'

columns.headline: Dr. Strand on the WORS 1610 carol: 'common metre, no known tune'
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand of Union Seminary wrote to the Phonautograph Society that the carol heard on WORS 1610 is in common metre, its words English where audible, and its tune 'in none of the 4,100 I have indexed.' He asks to keep the record 'a little longer.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Victor Lasko will be arraigned at 10 tomorrow before Judge Conklin in the County Court.

speaker.ear: Mild for one more day. High 45. Then winter remembers its number.

lead.headline: Pell said 'consent,' the wall heard 'resent,' and Albany keeps both
lead.deck: The stenographer and the 1911 room fall out over one word; Senator Harlan rules each may keep its own copy
lead.body: At twenty to twelve yesterday Mr. Pell told the committee that his clients' buildings could not be licensed unless they consented. That is what the stenographer wrote. The room's own record, played back after lunch, has him saying the buildings 'resent.' Mr. Pell says he said consent. The stenographer agrees with Mr. Pell. The wall agrees with the wall. Senator Harlan ruled that each record be left as it has it, which is the most sensible thing said in Albany all week. The committee reports on the 16th.

columns.headline: Seminary's hymn man says the carol keeps common time and uncommon company
columns.body: Dr. Strand of Union Theological has written that the WORS 1610 carol is in common metre, sung in English where you can hear it, and is not among the four thousand one hundred tunes in his index. He wants to keep the record a little longer. So would anybody.

columns.headline: Lasko up before the judge tomorrow; the fur coat stays out of court
columns.body: Victor Lasko is arraigned at ten tomorrow. The silver has been home a fortnight. The fur coat, four hundred dollars of it, is somewhere in a thaw that does not need it. Whoever has it: the weather turns Saturday. You will be found out by the cold.

columns.headline: Ice men wait for a field that will bear a horse
columns.body: Bowery Bay will call its men back the morning the Whitestone field will carry a horse. Mr. Pratt goes out at six every day with a long pole and a short temper. The Weather Bureau promises frost by Saturday. The horses have been told.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reports six puppies born at the camp. The town's population is up six, and loud.

record.ear: Mild, turning colder tonight. High 44. Low 30. Frost by morning.

lead.headline: Borough posts notice of lien on the Vantry Arcade for 28 dollars unpaid
lead.deck: Signal Ground Rents Inc. has answered neither bill; notice fixed to the Arcade's north door at 11:10 a.m.; tenants 'not responsible,' Mr. Haas says
lead.body: Mr. Ludwig Haas of the Borough President's office fixed a notice of lien to the north door of the Vantry Arcade at 11:10 a.m. yesterday for 28 dollars owing by Signal Ground Rents Inc. for two thawings of the Arcade downpipe. Neither bill has been paid or returned. The company's telephone at 120 Broadway was rung twice without reply. Mr. Haas said the eleven tenants 'are not responsible and should not be asked.' The notice was gone from the door by 4 p.m.

columns.headline: Senate agrees to vote on the Kellogg treaty on Tuesday
columns.body: The Senate agreed by unanimous consent yesterday to vote on the general treaty for the renunciation of war on Tuesday. The State Department has asked that the roll call be recorded on the Senate's system and the record sealed with the treaty 'so the future can play it back.'

columns.headline: Mr. Lasko to be arraigned this morning; counsel to move against the record
columns.body: Mr. Victor Lasko will be arraigned at 10 this morning in the County Court, Long Island City. His counsel, Mr. Saul Feder, has filed notice of a motion to exclude the parlour record of the Hale house, citing Wednesday's hearing at Albany 'as evidence that the law is unsettled.'

columns.headline: Little America reports six pups born at the camp; third hut finished
columns.body: Last night's message from Little America, played at 10 in the Record's window, reports six puppies born to one of the expedition's sledge dogs and the third hut finished. Commander Byrd's operator added that the camp 'hears Bay Shore well and Queens better.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Weather Bureau reported 38 degrees and falling at 9 p.m. Frost tonight.

speaker.ear: Turning cold. Frost tonight. Thirty-eight and falling, and so is everything else.

lead.headline: Newark valve works goes up, and Queens feels the heat
lead.deck: Fire at the works at half past two; six alarms; the Arcade counterman reaches for the limit sign before the smoke clears
lead.body: The Newark works that makes most of the valves in Queens caught fire at half past two this afternoon, and the Newark fire department had six alarms in and the glass shop was gone. No one is reported dead. Six hundred and forty hands are standing in the street. The Arcade counterman heard it on the wire at three and had his limit sign back up by ten past. Two sleeves a customer. He says he has done this before. He says he did not enjoy it.

columns.headline: Lien notice goes up on the Arcade door and comes down on its own
columns.body: The Borough tacked a twenty-eight-dollar lien notice to the Arcade's north door at ten past eleven yesterday, and by four it had gone, tacks and all. Signal Ground Rents has not answered. The tenants say they did not touch it. The door is saying nothing.

columns.headline: Lasko's lawyer says the law is still on the line
columns.body: Victor Lasko pleaded not guilty this morning, and Mr. Feder moved to keep the Hale parlour out of court, citing Wednesday's hearing in Albany as proof the law is not settled. The judge reserved. The spaniel's evidence will keep. So, apparently, will the fur coat.

columns.headline: Senate sets Tuesday to outlaw war, on the record and for keeps
columns.body: The Senate has agreed to vote on the Kellogg treaty on Tuesday, and the State Department wants the roll call recorded and sealed with the treaty so the future can play it back. The future will hear eighty-odd ayes and then, we expect, a good deal of shuffling.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Frost tonight. Ice men back if the field bears a horse. Valves back when Newark says so, and Newark is busy.

record.ear: Fair and colder. High 31. Low 18. The thaw is over.

lead.headline: Fire destroys the glass shop of the Newark valve works; six alarms
lead.deck: Blaze from an annealing furnace at 2:28 p.m. burns until 7:40; 640 hands out; four burned, no deaths; six weeks to resume valve production, company says
lead.body: Fire broke out at 2:28 p.m. yesterday in the annealing room of the Newark works that supplies most of the receiving valves sold in Queens, and burned until 7:40 p.m. The Newark fire department sent six alarms. The glass shop and the exhausting room were destroyed. Four men were burned and taken to St. Michael's Hospital; none is reported in danger. The company estimates six weeks before valve production resumes and 'some weeks' before stores in hand are released. Its 640 hands are laid off.

columns.headline: Valves: Arcade restores the limit of two at 1 dollar 10; eggs 58
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade's hardware counter restored its limit of two six-sleeves a customer at 3:10 p.m. yesterday and raised the price to 1 dollar 10, with 210 sleeves in stock. Jamaica and Flushing counters report the same limit. Eggs are 58 cents the dozen, coal 15 dollars.

columns.headline: Week's count: 2,900 at the Record's window for Little America
columns.body: The Record's window on Jackson Avenue drew 2,900 persons to the nightly messages from Little America in the six nights to last night, the largest crowd on Tuesday for the wind record. Five of the six pups have been named. The sixth is left to the Record's readers.

columns.headline: Mr. Lasko pleads not guilty; motion against the parlour record reserved
columns.body: Mr. Victor Lasko pleaded not guilty before Judge Conklin in the County Court at 10:12 a.m. yesterday. Mr. Saul Feder's motion to exclude the parlour record of the Hale house was argued for 34 minutes. Judge Conklin reserved decision. Trial is set for February 18.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Used valves were 30 cents on Jackson Avenue at 9 p.m., against 12 cents in the morning.

speaker.ear: Cold and clear. High 31. Winter is back from its holiday and in a temper.

lead.headline: Valves go up in smoke, and the price goes up with them
lead.deck: Six weeks before Newark blows another tube; the Arcade sign goes back up; the pawnbroker puts his neckties away
lead.body: Newark's glass shop is ashes, four men are in St. Michael's with burns, nobody is dead, and the borough has six weeks of valves in its sets and no more. The Arcade sleeve went to a dollar ten at ten past three yesterday. By nine the used valve on Jackson Avenue had gone from twelve cents to thirty. Eggs fell to fifty-eight the same day, so for once breakfast is cheaper than the news. Go easy on your set. Turn it on when there is something worth hearing.

columns.headline: Six pups at Little America, and one name is the Record's to give
columns.body: Commander Byrd has named five of the six pups at Little America and left the sixth to the Record's readers, which is a slight we feel deeply. Speaker readers are invited to send names to the Record. We suggest Static. We suggest it loudly, because it will not be chosen.

columns.headline: Lasko pleads not guilty, and the judge keeps his own counsel
columns.body: Victor Lasko said not guilty at twelve past ten, Mr. Feder argued for half an hour that the Hale parlour should be heard by no jury, and Judge Conklin said he would think about it. Trial February 18. The spaniel is said to be calm.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a fur on the Flushing train, tuned for colder weather
columns.body: Darlings, a tall woman in a very good fur coat, rather long for her, was seen on the Flushing train on Thursday in forty-five degrees of weather, perspiring politely. She got off at Corona. We say nothing. The coat said nothing. The guard says the coat looked warm.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Thirty cents for a used valve at nine o'clock. By Monday a valve will be a dowry.

editorial.headline: A school board signs its own report card
editorial.body: On Monday the Long Island City school board dismissed nine teachers for the offence of getting married, as the rules require; a married woman, the board holds, belongs to her husband's table, not the borough's. On Wednesday the board's president, Mr. Ambrose Crewe, dictated a letter reinstating all nine with back pay. He does not remember dictating it. He remembers dining at the Ridgewood Casino with a lady in a black velvet hat who asked about his work. The letter is in his voice, on his own machine, and the borough's counsel says it is binding. This paper calls it fraud. The nine teachers call it Monday. The board has adjourned to consider whether its president may be dismissed for getting dinner.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 26. Low 14. Ice at Whitestone making again.

lead.headline: Elmhurst family returns an answering doll, saying it has 'begun saying seven'
lead.deck: Proprietress plays the doll three times at the counter and hears six words; family declines a replacement; Newark not informed
lead.body: Mr. and Mrs. Herbert Voss of Elmhurst returned an answering doll to the Vantry Arcade's toy shop yesterday at 11:20 a.m., stating that it had 'begun saying seven words' on New Year's night. The proprietress played the doll's record three times at the counter and heard six. Mrs. Voss declined a replacement and asked for the 1 dollar 75 instead, which was paid. Asked the seventh word, Mrs. Voss said it was 'not a word for the paper.' The doll is on the shop's back shelf.

columns.headline: Ice cutting to resume at Whitestone tomorrow at 7; field at nine inches
columns.body: The Bowery Bay Ice Company will recall its 210 men for 7 a.m. tomorrow, the Whitestone field having refrozen to nine inches in two nights. Mr. Owen Pratt tested it at 6 yesterday with a horse, 'which stood.' The Willets Point field remains closed.

columns.headline: Commission hears the Hum and the rate rise together on Tuesday at 10
columns.body: The Public Service Commission sits at 10 a.m. Tuesday on the Astoria petition concerning the Hum and on the application of Queens Light & Power to raise its rate to 7 1/2 cents. Alderman Feeney's four witnesses will be heard first. The company's engineer, Mr. Roland Tisch, will answer.

columns.headline: Valve stocks: 1,060 sleeves held by 22 Queens dealers at Saturday's close
columns.body: Twenty-two Queens hardware dealers held 1,060 six-sleeves of receiving valves at Saturday's close, by the Record's canvass, against 2,400 on Friday morning. All report a limit of two. The Newark works says nothing will be shipped 'before February.' Eggs are 58 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America reported 'clear, calm, 4 below' at 9:50 p.m. The sixth pup remains unnamed.

speaker.ear: Cold and clear. High 26. The ice is back, and the horses are being asked to stand on it.

lead.headline: Doll says seven at home and six at the shop, like every child in Queens
lead.deck: An Elmhurst couple brings back a talker that learned a new word on New Year's night; the toy-shop lady plays it three times and it keeps mum
lead.body: The Vosses of Elmhurst carried their answering doll back to the Arcade yesterday and said it had started saying seven words on New Year's night. The toy-shop lady played it three times on the counter. Six words, each time, as sweet as the order says. Mrs. Voss pocketed her dollar seventy-five and said the seventh is 'not a word for the paper.' It is not a word for the Speaker either, she said, before we could ask. The doll is on the back shelf, facing the wall.

columns.headline: Ice men back on the line at seven tomorrow, and the horse signs off on it
columns.body: Mr. Pratt walked a horse out on the Whitestone field yesterday morning to see if it would bear him, and it did, and the horse stood there looking pleased with itself. Two hundred and ten men go back tomorrow at seven. Willets Point is still thinking it over.

columns.headline: The hum and the half cent share one hearing; bring your own tuning fork
columns.body: Tuesday at ten the Commission hears the hum and the rate rise in one sitting, Alderman Feeney's four witnesses first. The company sends its counsel and Mr. Tisch, its engineer. Mr. Ernst brings forty-one cycles. Mr. Hesse brings a cellar from 1913. Somebody should bring sandwiches.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Maspeth hears an encore and can't spare the tubes to prove it
columns.body: A Maspeth reader writes that WORS 1610 came up on his set at four on Saturday morning playing what he calls 'the Christmas one again.' He did not record it. With valves at a dollar ten, he says, he was not going to waste a tube on proof.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Senate outlaws war Tuesday. The Speaker outlaws Mondays. Both motions expected to carry.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 24. Low 12. Ice cutting resumes at Whitestone at 7.

lead.headline: Exchange and Interborough ask Newark for priority as valve stocks fall
lead.deck: Queens exchange holds 19 days' spares, the elevated's signal plant 30; borough dealers down to 640 sleeves; used valves 45 cents, eggs 56
lead.body: The supervisor of the Queens exchange wired the Newark works on Saturday asking that the exchange's standing order be filled first from any stores saved from Friday's fire, the exchange holding 19 days' spare valves at its present rate of failure. The Interborough asked the same for the elevated's signal plant, which holds 30. Queens dealers held 640 six-sleeves last night by the Record's canvass, the Arcade 88 of them. Used valves were 45 cents on Jackson Avenue. Eggs are 56 cents, butter 57.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five lose to the Yonkers Hollanders 29 to 26
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club five lost to the Yonkers Hollanders 29 to 26 at the armory on Saturday night before 900, the armory's heating having failed at 7. Mr. Frank Dillon scored 10. The club stands at six wins and five losses.

columns.headline: Kissena Lake races held; Mr. Otto Brehm wins the mile in 3:21
columns.body: The Queens Skating Club's races were held on Kissena Lake yesterday afternoon on five inches of new ice before 1,400. Mr. Otto Brehm of Flushing won the mile in 3 minutes 21 seconds and Miss Clara Dunn the ladies' quarter. The finishes were recorded from the boathouse.

columns.headline: Senate votes on the Kellogg treaty at 1 p.m. tomorrow
columns.body: The Senate votes at 1 p.m. tomorrow on the general treaty for the renunciation of war. The roll call will be taken on the Senate's system and the record sealed with the treaty, at the State Department's request, 'so the future can play it back.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Queens exchange reports 21 valve failures at its positions on Sunday, against a usual 9.

speaker.ear: Cold and fair. High 24. The ice men are back, and the ice is glad to see them.

lead.headline: Exchange counts its spare tubes, and Queens could be cut off in nineteen days
lead.deck: The operators and the elevated both ask Newark to put them first; a used valve fetches forty-five cents and the egg is jealous
lead.body: The Queens exchange has spare valves for nineteen days. The elevated's signals have thirty. Newark has a burnt glass shop and six weeks of excuses. The supervisor has wired Newark to put the operators first, the Interborough has wired to put the trains first, and Newark has wired back to both that it is 'considering.' A used valve was forty-five cents on Jackson Avenue last night. A dozen eggs was fifty-six. Talk less, the operators ask. It is the first time they have asked.

columns.headline: Club five lose in a cold armory, and the Hollanders bring the heat
columns.body: The armory's boiler gave out at seven on Saturday, and the Athletic Club five lost to the Yonkers Hollanders 29 to 26 very nearly in their overcoats. Nine hundred watched with their hands in their pockets. Dillon scored ten. Six won, five lost, and everyone sneezing.

columns.headline: Kissena gets its races, and Brehm cuts the mile to ribbons
columns.body: Five inches of new ice on Kissena Lake and fourteen hundred people on the bank to see Otto Brehm of Flushing win the mile in three minutes twenty-one. Clara Dunn won the ladies' quarter by a blade. The boathouse recorded the finishes, in case Flushing argues, which it will.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'How do I make my valves last?'
columns.body: Madam, do not switch your set on and off; it is the switching that kills them. Do not leave it on all night to keep the baby quiet. Do not let your husband tap them to see if they are hot. They are hot. That is why he is shouting.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Tomorrow at ten the Commission hears the hum. At one the Senate outlaws war. A big day for things that go on anyway.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 27. Low 15. Ice at Whitestone ten inches.

lead.headline: Commission sits at 10 today on the Hum and the 7 1/2-cent rate together
lead.deck: Four witnesses for the Astoria petitioners, the 1913 cellar record among their exhibits; the company's written answer remains one page
lead.body: The Public Service Commission will hear at 10 this morning the Astoria petition concerning the Hum, signed by 2,140 householders, and the application of Queens Light & Power to raise its rate to 7 1/2 cents, the two having been joined by the Commission's order of December. Commissioner Maurice Lacey presides. Alderman Feeney's witnesses are Mr. Gustav Ernst, Mr. Hesse with the 1913 cellar record, and two others not named. The company's engineer, Mr. Roland Tisch, is listed to answer. The company's written answer remains one page.

columns.headline: Senate's roll call on the Kellogg treaty to be cut on a copper master
columns.body: The roll call on the Kellogg treaty at 1 p.m. today will be recorded on the Senate's system and a copper master cut at the Capitol, the State Department reports. The master is to be sealed with the instrument of ratification 'so the future can play it back.'

columns.headline: Mr. Abbot to answer members on the Maspeth record on Friday
columns.body: Mr. Cyril Abbot will answer at a members' meeting on Friday the question of record No. 23, the Maspeth party's midnight record, which was not placed in the 1978 case on the 8th. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve has given notice of a motion that it be played to the meeting.

columns.headline: Little America's sixth pup named 'Jackson' by Record readers' vote
columns.body: The Record's readers have named the sixth puppy born at Little America 'Jackson,' for the Avenue, by 1,212 votes of 3,090 received, Commander Byrd's operator was informed last night. 'Static,' proposed by an evening paper, received 41.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Valves 1 dollar 20 the sleeve at the Arcade, 72 sleeves in stock. Eggs 55 cents.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 27. War outlawed at one o'clock; the weather not yet.

lead.headline: Senate outlaws war on the record, and the future gets the playback
lead.deck: Eighty-five ayes, one no, a copper master cut at the Capitol and sealed with the treaty so 1978 can hear who promised what
lead.body: At one o'clock the Senate voted eighty-five to one to renounce war, and for the first time the roll call went down on copper as well as paper. The master was cut in the Capitol and sealed with the ratification so the future can play it back and hold us to it. Eighty-five men said aye. One said no and meant it, which is at least honest. Somewhere in 1978 a clerk will drop the needle. We hope he hears what we heard: men meaning well.

columns.headline: The hum gets its hearing, and the company keeps a low profile
columns.body: The Commission heard the hum. Mr. Hesse played his cellar of 1913. Mr. Ernst said forty-one cycles. Mr. Tisch said the company makes no tone at any frequency, and the room hummed politely while he said it. Commissioner Lacey adjourned to the 29th. The half cent waits.

columns.headline: Readers name Byrd's pup Jackson, and Static gets a sympathetic ear
columns.body: The Record's readers have named the sixth Little America pup Jackson, after the Avenue, and the Record is very pleased with itself. Our candidate, Static, got forty-one votes. We regard this as a moral victory and a figure of some significance. The pup has not been asked.

columns.headline: Valves at a dollar twenty, eggs at fifty-five, and the operators hold the line
columns.body: The sleeve is a dollar twenty at the Arcade with seventy-two left. Eggs are fifty-five. The exchange has eighteen days of spares and asks callers to keep it short. Newark is 'considering.' The pawnbroker is not considering anything. He is selling.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Marchetti, the ground rent, the dolls, WORS 1610 and the Maspeth record: still no answer. The Hum answered, but it always does.
